When a county grows quickly, does it also gain a large number of residents?
Not always. A small county can grow faster in percentage terms while a larger
county adds more people. That distinction matters when local governments think
about housing, transportation, and public services.

Living in Philadelphia made me curious about changes across the rest of the
state. News about a fast-growing county can sound like a story about a large
number of new residents, but the percentage alone does not tell us that.
I wanted to see how much the comparison changes when I look at the number of
people as well. Pennsylvania offers a useful example because its counties
range from small rural communities to large urban areas.

I use Census Bureau estimates for all 67 Pennsylvania counties to compare
population change from the April 1, 2020 estimates base to July 1, 2024. This
is the same Vintage 2024 dataset I used in Blog 5. Here I use an interactive
chart to let readers examine individual counties and compare two ways to
measure growth. The Census Bureau has since released newer estimates; I keep
the 2024 vintage so the comparison stays consistent with my earlier post.

## Explore the counties

Each dot represents a county. The horizontal axis shows its 2020 population
on a logarithmic scale, so the gap between 10,000 and 100,000 is the same
width as the gap between 100,000 and 1 million. Choose a measure to switch
between percentage change and the number of people gained or lost. Hover over
a dot to see the county name, population at both endpoints, and both measures
of change. You can also select a county to highlight it, or click a legend
label to show or hide gainers or losers.

## What changes when we switch measures?

Pike County had the fastest percentage growth in the state: its population
rose by about 6.5%, or 3,831 people. Chester County grew by a smaller 4.9%,
but added 26,327 people. Chester started with about nine times as many
residents, so its smaller rate still meant a much larger increase in people.
Switching the chart to “Change in people” makes that difference visible.

Montgomery and Cumberland offer another comparison. Cumberland grew by about
6.2%, while Montgomery grew by about 2.7%. Yet Montgomery added 22,777
residents, compared with 16,048 in Cumberland. Montgomery began with more
than three times Cumberland's population. If I ranked counties only by growth
rate, I would miss how many more residents Montgomery gained. If I ranked them
only by the number gained, I would miss how quickly Cumberland changed
relative to its starting size. The two measures answer different questions,
and the switch in the chart lets the reader see both for every county.

The chart also shows why the state total can be misleading about local
experience. Pennsylvania added about 75,842 residents overall, but 39 counties
lost population. Philadelphia lost 29,878 residents, or about 1.9% of its
2020 base. Select Philadelphia to find it among the other counties, then
switch measures to compare the size of its loss with the losses elsewhere.

## Takeaway

For a county planner, a percentage helps compare the pace of change across
places of different sizes. The number of people may matter more when
estimating demand for homes or services. Neither number alone tells a planner
how many homes to build: household size, vacancies, and population age also
matter. The chart describes where changes occurred; it does not show why
people moved or trace moves between counties.

## Data and reproduction

The data come from the [Census Bureau's Vintage 2024 county population
estimates](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-kits/2025/population-estimates-components-change-counties-metro-micro-puerto-rico.html).
The starting value is the estimates base, not the unadjusted 2020 census
count. The Bureau can revise earlier estimates when it releases a new vintage.
I calculate the change as the 2024 estimate minus the base and divide by the
base for the percentage change.

The chart uses Plotly's JavaScript library. The [county data](data/pa-counties.csv),
[preparation code](code/prepare.R), [chart code](code/chart.js), and
[reproduction instructions](README.md) are available with the post. The
source CSV comes from the checked output of [Blog 5](../post5/index.html); its guide
explains how to download and prepare the original Census data.
